newsitem.title: USA: Economists see 1997 US jobless rate below 5.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: Economists see 1997 US jobless rate below 5.0 pct.

text.p: The last time U.S. unemployment rates were consistently below 5.0 percent the New York Jets consistently fielded winning football teams.

In 1969, the last time the Jets appeared in a Super Bowl, U.S. unemployment averaged just 3.5 percent. This year it seems likely unemployment levels will sink below 5.0 percent, economists said, the lowest in more than two decades.
While such rates are welcome news for job seekers, economists warned that they have more ominous implications for the overall economy in the form of higher inflation.

"In 1973 we averaged 4.9 percent and moved up to 5.6 percent with the recession in 1974. We've never averaged below 5.0 percent since," said Donald Ratajczak, director of economic forecasting at Georgia State University. "This year we could well see levels below 5.0 percent."

Averages below 5.0 percent were common in the 1960s economists said, but levels that low could threaten the current climate of contained inflation and strong growth. Unemployment currently runs at 5.4 percent.
"(A) risk to the bond market is the possibility that the unemployment rate could drop sharply in the near future," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
Iggo said nonfarm payrolls grew by more than 2.0 percent in 1996 while the unemployment rate edged down only slightly due to a sharp acceleration in labor force growth.

"The labor force grew by over 2.0 percent in the past year, twice the 1995 pace and twice as fast as the growth rate of the working age population. Labor force growth has been especially strong the last during the past three months," Iggo said.
Should some of this strength be reversed in the months ahead, a rapid fall -- perhaps as much as 0.5 percent -- in the unemployment rate would occur, Iggo said.
The uncertainty ahead lies in how the Federal Reserve reacts to the growing divergence between wage and price inflation at a time when the economy continues to expand.

"During 1996, average hourly earnings rose 3.8 percent," Iggo said, pointing out that increase represented an acceleration of almost a full percentage point. In contrast, he added, the core consumer price index (CPI) excluding the volatile food and energy components "slowed by almost half a point to 2.6 percent."
Average hourly earnings have accelerated each of the past four years while core CPI mostly had slowed.

"During those years, falling benefits costs have enabled firms to hold overall compensation costs down, making it easier to hold the line on prices," Iggo said. However, he said the divergence between wages and prices had been sustained by faster productivity growth and lower profit margins -- neither of which will continue.
"Benefits are the issue. We saw only a 2.0 percent rise in 1996 but group insurance surveys are projecting as much as 10 percent increases in 1997," said Georgia State's Ratajczak.
David Levy, director of forecasting at the Jerome Levy Economics Institute at Bard College, said unemployment levels below 5.0 percent were possible.

"Some of the numbers now may be a little padded because people who had been out of the market -- like early retirees -- had been lured back. Levy expected unemployment rates in the 5.0 or better vicinity for most of the year, but said it wasn't unreasonable to expect lower levels.
He credited the Fed with recognizing it wasn't dealing with the same set of economic problems it had five or 10 years ago as the usual roadmaps do not apply at this juncture.
"They now have built enough credibility to sit and watch a situation rather than act well in advance," Levy said.
